1. The weather: il fait, il pleut, il y a
For the weather French uses three impersonal constructions, all with “il”, like “it” in English.
Il fait beau / mauvais / chaud / froid / doux.
It’s nice / bad / hot / cold / mild.
Il y a du soleil / du vent / des nuages / du brouillard.
The question: “Quel temps fait-il ?” (What’s the weather like?). Spoken: “Il fait quel temps ?”. And “Il fait combien ?” = “How many degrees is it?”.
Don’t say “il est chaud” for the weather: “il est chaud” means a person is hot (or keen). For the weather: “il fait chaud”. For yourself: “j’ai chaud” (I’m hot), “j’ai froid” (I’m cold).
The simplest French future uses the verb ALLER (chapter 4) + an infinitive. It’s exactly like English “going to”: “je vais partir” = “I’m going to leave”.
The negation goes around ALLER: “Je ne vais pas sortir” (I’m not going to go out). With reflexive verbs, the pronoun stays next to the infinitive: “Je vais me coucher” (I’m going to go to bed).
For the weather: “Il va faire beau” (It’s going to be nice), “Il va pleuvoir” (It’s going to rain), “Il va y avoir du vent” (It’s going to be windy).
Watch the context: “Je vais à Paris” = “I’m going to Paris” (movement), but “Je vais visiter Paris” = “I’m going to visit Paris” (future).
The rule is about pronunciation: before a vowel, “en” (en été, en automne, en hiver). “Printemps” starts with a consonant, so “au printemps”.
Unlike English, seasons and months are written with a small letter.
“In” a month = “en” or “au mois de”: “en mai” = “au mois de mai” (in May).
The date is given with “le” + cardinal number (not ordinal!) + month:
It’s the 14th of July. (France’s national day)
My birthday is on the 1st of March.
Exception: the first day of the month uses the ordinal: “le premier mai” (1er mai), but “le deux mai”, “le trois mai”.
The question: “Quelle est la date aujourd’hui ?” or, spoken, “On est le combien aujourd’hui ?”.
“Dans” + a duration = “in” (future): “dans deux heures” = “in two hours’ time”. Don’t confuse it with “depuis” (chapter 7) = “for / since (past up to now)”.
il y a + partitive: du vent.

In the evening Brigitte serves the tartiflette. Everyone eats a lot. Pierre talks about his bread, Manon about her school, and Pompon the dog sleeps by the fireplace.
